passage: Sunday night. My daughter Irawati came home with a new phrase, "that's so mid", and a new circle from art class, Meher and Ishaan and a girl everyone calls Sunny. They hummed a song I have never heard. At lunch I laughed and said, "Mid? Like middle?" Her fork stopped. She took her plate to her room. I felt stupid. Tonight I knocked and asked her to teach me three of the new words. She rolled her eyes, but she taught me, and then told me Meher does funny voices and Ishaan draws maps of imaginary towns. Note to self: ask, do not mock. She is still the same girl. — Sangeeta

Dilnaz noticed first because of the songs. Her son Faiz, who used to hum old film tunes while feeding the goats, now played loud rap from Chetan's phone on the verandah of their house in the kasba. He said “bro” to everyone, even his grandfather.
At dinner her husband snorted. “Chetan's gang has turned you into a parrot.” Faiz pushed his plate away and went to the roof.
Dilnaz took two cups of chai up later. She sat without speaking for a while. Then she asked, “The song with the drums, who sings it?” Faiz looked at her, surprised, and started to explain, words tumbling out. Below, Chetan's whistle came from the lane. Faiz said, “Can he come in for tea tomorrow?” She said yes.

qa.q: Where did Faiz go after his father's remark?
qa.a: He went to the roof.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz hope for when she took chai up to the roof?
qa.a: She felt concerned but curious, hoping to reconnect with Faiz by asking about his music instead of scolding.

qa.q: Which response worked better with Faiz, and why?
qa.a: Dilnaz's calm question worked better than his father's mocking, because it made Faiz want to talk and even bring Chetan home.

qa.q: How might Faiz have felt when his father called him a parrot?
qa.a: He probably felt humiliated and defensive, which is why he pushed his plate away and left.

grounding: A mother notices her teen's new music, slang and friend circle and chooses steady curiosity, while ridicule pushes him away.

subtype: Sudden shifts in taste and friends [Observer]
passage:
Chen noticed the changes one grey Saturday in their Toronto apartment. His daughter Mei now wore her hair in braids like her new friend Nkechi, played Afrobeats while doing homework, and ended texts with “periodt”.
His first joke almost slipped out at breakfast: “Are you still Chinese?” He stopped himself, remembering how his own father had mocked his skateboarding friends.
Instead, he asked, “This song, who is it?” Mei blinked, then played three more, explaining the rhythms. That afternoon Nkechi and another girl, Hana, came over. Chen made scallion pancakes and listened more than he talked. When they left, Mei said, “You were actually normal, Ba.” He decided that counted as praise.

qa.q: Which city was the family's apartment in?
qa.a: It was in Toronto.

qa.q: How can you tell Chen felt uneasy about the changes at first?
qa.a: A mocking joke almost slipped out at breakfast, which shows he felt unsettled and a little left behind by Mei's new style and friends.

qa.q: What did Chen do that others could learn from?
qa.a: He held back the joke, asked about the music with real interest, and welcomed Mei's friends home, which kept Mei talking to him.

qa.q: How might Mei have felt when her father asked about the song?
qa.a: She seemed surprised and pleased to be asked, since she played three more and explained them eagerly.

grounding: A father notices his teen's new music, style and friends, resists ridicule and chooses curiosity, which draws her closer.

passage: In the school hall at the parent-teacher meeting, Hansa waited with her daughter Jahnavi on the plastic chairs, and noticed how much had changed in three months. Jahnavi's old friend Pinky was sitting across the hall with her mother, but Jahnavi didn't look at her. Instead she kept waving at three girls near the door, all with the same short haircut she'd had done last month. She said 'no cap' and 'lowkey' in every sentence, and one earbud played music Hansa had never heard. Hansa's first thought was to joke about her daughter's 'new language'. She didn't. She asked, 'Who are they? Tell me about them.' Jahnavi hesitated, then talked about them all the way to the class teacher's table, and even let Hansa hear the song.

qa.a: Curiosity kept Jahnavi talking and even sharing the song, while ridicule could have pushed her further into the group and away from Hansa.
